pages.name: Introduction
pages.html:
Introduction

Students are now ready to learn the Five Phonetic Skills. These Five Phonetic Skills help students learn likely and unlikely sequences of letters. In the past, students have been asked to sound words phonetically and have applied sight words adequately. Now they must “prove” the word.

Scientifically Based Method

The Reading Horizons method is a scientifically based method. It is explicit, systematic, sequential phonics taught through multi-sensory, direct instruction.

Delivery Method
  • Have the students stand at whiteboards or chalkboards
  • Dictate the letter, sound, or word twice to the students
  • Use your hands to draw attention to your mouth
  • Students repeat twice and write once on the board
  • Students benefit from active engagement
  • The delivery method employs their auditory, visual, tactile, and kinesthetic modalities

pages.name: Decoding Skill # 1
pages.html:
Decoding Skill # 1
  • Marking the words from left to right, Mark everything under the word.
  • Look at the first vowel and determine how many consonants follow it.
  • If there is only one, that consonant will move to the next syllable.
  • The syllable break will be between the vowel and the consonant. And every syllable must have a working vowel.
  • Now apply the Five Phonetic Skills to decode each syllable separately.
  • At this point, guardians are no longer marked.
Robot
Marked Example
Tiger
Marked Example
Pupil
Marked Example
When a vowel is followed by just one consonant, that consonant must go forward and join with the next vowel. (one guardian goes on)

pages.name: Decoding Skill # 2
pages.html:
Decoding Skill # 2
  • Marking the words from left to right, Mark everything under the word.
  • Look at the first vowel and determine how many consonants follow it.
  • If there are two, they will split.
  • The syllable break will be between those two consonants. And every syllable must have a working vowel.
  • Now apply the Five Phonetic Skills to decode each syllable separately.
  • At this point, guardians are no longer marked.

consonant
Marked Example
translate
Marked Example
When a vowel is followed by two consonants, they will split. (two guardians split).

pages.name: Murmur Diphthongs
pages.subtitle: Introduction
pages.html:
Murmur Diphthongs
Introduction

A Diphthong is a vowel blend. A Murmur Diphthong is a vowel blended with an R. Murmur diphthongs are vowel combinations followed by the letter r, where the vowel sound blends with the r sound to make a new sound: ar in car, or in fork, er in her, ir in bird, ur in turn.

  • They are also known as r-controlled vowels.
  • Murmur Diphthongs are predictable vowel sounds that are neither long nor short.
  • To mark a Murmur Diphthong, place an X under the vowel and arc the two letters together

pages.name: Murmur Diphthongs
pages.subtitle: AR • OR • ER, IR, UR
pages.html:
Murmur Diphthongs
AR • OR • ER, IR, UR
AR Murmur Diphthong
  • The AR Murmur Diphthong has a sound like the name of the letter R.
car
Marked Example
far
Marked Example
park
Marked Example
OR Murmur Diphthong

The OR Murmur Diphthong sounds like the word “or.”

sort
Marked Example
fort
Marked Example
ER, IR, UR Murmur Diphthongs

The ER, IR, UR Murmur Diphthongs all have the same sound of /er/. In words with the sound /er/, ER is the most frequent spelling.

her
Marked Example
sir
Marked Example
fur
Marked Example

pages.name: Adding Suffixes To Murmur Diphthongs
pages.html:
Adding Suffixes To Murmur Diphthongs

To add suffixes to Murmur Diphthongs, there must be two consonants between the vowel and the suffix.

morn morning
Marked Example

If the Murmur Diphthong ends the word, add the letter R before adding the suffix.

scar scarring

pages.name: Murmur Diphthong Exceptions
pages.html:
Murmur Diphthong Exceptions

When Silent E follows directly after a Murmur Diphthong, the word follows Phonetic Skill 4.

fire
Marked Example

If adjacent vowels precede a Murmur Diphthong, the word follows Phonetic Skill 5.

Fear
Marked Example
air
Marked Example

Whenever W, or the sound of W, precedes the vowel A or O, it changes the vowel sound.

Ward
Marked Example
work
Marked Example

Murmur Diphthong ER and OR takes the sound short /a/ or /ar/ when at the end of a word or when used as a suffix.

Helper
Marked Example
educator
Marked Example

pages.name: Special Vowel Sounds
pages.subtitle: Introduction
pages.html:
Special Vowel Sounds
Introduction

Special Vowel Sounds are Diphthongs. A diphthong is a combination of two vowel sounds that are pronounced together in one syllable. Examples: oi in coin, oy in boy, ou in house, ow in cow.

When proving words with Special Vowel Sounds, put an X between the vowels and arc them together

AU, AW

The first two Special Vowel Sounds have the sound /or/. If the sound comes in the middle of a word, the correct spelling must be memorized. But, if the sound comes at the end of the word, it will be spelled AW.

OU, OW

These Special Vowel Sounds have the sound / aw /. If the sound comes in the middle of the word, the correct spelling must be memorized. If the sound is at the end of the word, it will be spelled OW. Sometimes, OW can say the sound of long O

pages.name: Special Vowel Sounds
pages.subtitle: OI, OY • OO, OO • UE, EW, EU
pages.html:
Special Vowel Sounds
OI, OY • OO, OO • UE, EW, EU
OI, OY

These Special Vowel Sounds make the sound /oy/. The only time OY comes in the middle of word is in coined words. Otherwise, the OY Special Vowel Sound will always come at the ends of words and syllables

OO, OO

These two Special Vowel Sounds are spelled the same but have different sounds. The first has the sound /oo/ like in the word “zoo”. The second has the sound /oo/ as in the word “look.”

UE, EW, EU

These Special Vowel Sounds make the sound / ew /. Sometimes UE will sound long u in a word and will follow phonetic skill five. The correct spelling must be memorized

pages.name: Prefixes
pages.html:
Prefixes

A prefix is a group of letters added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning. Examples: un- in unhappy, re- in rewrite, dis- in disagree, pre- in preview.

Common prefixes and their meanings
PrefixMeaningExampleMeaning of the word
un-not, oppositeunhappynot happy
re-againrewritewrite again
dis-removedisconnectseparate
pre-beforepreviewview before
Examples
  • happy → unhappy (not happy)
  • do → redo (do again)
  • agree → disagree (not agree)
  • heat → preheat (heat beforehand)
  • possible → impossible (not possible)
Remember

A prefix goes at the beginning of a word. A suffix goes at the end of a word (e.g., hope → hopeful, teach → teacher). A simple way to remember it is:

  • Prefix = before the root word
  • Suffix = after the root word

pages.name: Final _LE
pages.html:
Final _LE
  • The _LE ending has a schwa “ə“ or short U sound that precedes the sound of the letter L. The sound of the _LE ending is /ull/. _LE is a common ending syllable in English
  • The schwa is the most common vowel sound in English. It is the weak, unstressed sound often heard as /uh/. Final L's in English almost always have this sound
  • The sound can also be heard in some one-syllable words such as ‘mail’ or ‘sale’
  • To prove, Mark the E silent and write the symbol for the schwa sound right before the -LE ending
Apple

pages.name: Decoding Exception Words
pages.subtitle: Introduction
pages.html:
Decoding Exception Words
Introduction
  • The system of decoding you have just learned will work with most English words, but there are exceptions. There is a group of exceptions that are easy to handle. The word
  • “robin” when decoded properly should say /ro-bin/. So how do we handle this exception?
  • Avoid these words until the end of the method sequence. By this time, students are reading well enough that they can determine the proper pronunciation from context.
  • Teach students that any vowel marked long can be made short in pronunciation.
